decouverte.titre: The new member of the robotics club
paragraphes: Your robotics club needs a new member. This person will get the key to the room with the expensive tools.
The club does not choose at random. First, it writes down what the member must do. Then it asks what harm a mistake could cause.
In a company, checking a person before you give them access is called candidate screening.

decouverte.titre: The stronger the key, the more you check
decouverte.comme: To lend the key to the broom closet, you check almost nothing. For the key to the safe, you take much more care.
decouverte.enVrai: Each job gets a sensitivity level. It shows how much harm a person in that job could cause, on purpose or by mistake. NIST, a US standards group, calls this the risk designation. A higher level means a deeper check.

decouverte.question: Which job deserves the deepest check?
options: A person who welcomes visitors
An administrator who can open every database
An intern who tidies the supplies
decouverte.answer: An administrator who can open every database
decouverte.explanation: The more power a job gives over data, the more harm a mistake or a lie can do. The check must match that level.

decouverte.texte: A bank wants to hire an accountant. It runs a background check: it confirms the facts in the application. It looks at degrees, past jobs, criminal record and references. The job deals with the money of clients, so it also looks at the credit and money history of the person.

decouverte.titre: The social media of a candidate
decouverte.texte: A recruiter looks at the online profiles of a candidate. To keep this fair, the company has clear rules. The rules say what to look at and what to keep. The company also tells the candidate.

cards.question: Official definition: “background check”
cards.answer: Once a potential employee or contractor is identified, your organization should verify the information in their application and confirm their suitability for the position by conducting a background check.
cards.explanation: In simple words: check that the facts in the application are true. Check that the person is right for the job.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “background check” from memory.
cards.answer: Once a potential employee or contractor is identified, your organization should verify the information in their application and confirm their suitability for the position by conducting a background check.
cards.explanation: Two parts: verify the application, and confirm that the person fits the position.

cards.question: Official definition: “risk designation”
cards.answer: The classification or sensitivity assigned to a role (referred to as a risk designation by NIST, for example) should inform the types of authorizations an employee will receive once they are hired.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the sensitivity level of a job helps to decide which access the employee will get.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “risk designation” from memory.
cards.answer: The classification or sensitivity assigned to a role (referred to as a risk designation by NIST, for example) should inform the types of authorizations an employee will receive once they are hired.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the sensitivity of the role, the name risk designation, and the access that the employee gets.

cards.question: Besides helping to find the right person, what else is a clear job description for?
options: To measure the employee later against what was expected
To replace the employment contract
To set the salary of the employee
To decide alone which data and systems the employee can see
options_why: The contract is a different paper, signed by both sides.
Pay is decided in a different way. It is not the job of the description.
Access depends on how sensitive the job is, not on the description alone.
cards.answer: To measure the employee later against what was expected
cards.explanation: The description works like a ruler. Later, you compare what the employee does with what was promised.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Who should write the job description?
options: The security team, on its own
The new employee, on the first day
The finance team, on its own
The hiring manager, together with HR (human resources)
options_why: The security team does not know the daily tasks of the job. The manager and HR do.
The job must be described before anyone is hired.
Finance knows the budget, not the tasks of the job.
cards.answer: The hiring manager, together with HR (human resources)
cards.explanation: The manager knows the job. HR is the team that looks after employees, and it knows the hiring rules.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: What does the sensitivity level of a job depend on?
options: How much money the person will earn
How many years the person has studied
How much harm a person in that job could cause
How many people the person will manage
options_why: Pay is not the measure. A low-paid job can still reach very sensitive data.
Studies do not set the level. The possible harm does.
Managing people is not the measure. The possible harm is.
cards.answer: How much harm a person in that job could cause
cards.explanation: The bigger the possible harm, on purpose or by mistake, the higher the level.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”. NIST calls this level the risk designation.

cards.question: Which check may be added for highly sensitive jobs?
options: A look at the degrees of the person
A drug test or a deeper investigation
A call to the references of the person
A look at the work history
options_why: Degrees are part of the usual list, for most jobs.
References are part of the usual list, for most jobs.
Work history is part of the usual list, for most jobs.
cards.answer: A drug test or a deeper investigation
cards.explanation: The usual list covers education, work history and more. Very sensitive jobs may need more.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Which background check is BEST for a new administrator who can open every database?
options: A quick check, the same as for all new staff
No check, because the interview went well
A look at the social media profiles of the person only
A deep check that matches how sensitive the job is
options_why: The same check for everyone is simple, but it ignores the higher risk of this job.
An interview cannot confirm degrees, past jobs or a criminal record.
Social media shows only a small part of the picture.
cards.answer: A deep check that matches how sensitive the job is
cards.explanation: The check should match the security of the position. More access means more checking.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: A bank wants to hire a payroll manager. What should the bank do FIRST?
options: Write the job description and decide its sensitivity
Start the background check on the first good candidate
Give a new manager access to the payroll system
Post the job on social media sites
options_why: There is no candidate yet. The level of the check depends on the job, which comes first.
Access comes after hiring and checking, never before.
The bank should know the job and its sensitivity before it looks for people.
cards.answer: Write the job description and decide its sensitivity
cards.explanation: You must know the job and its risk before you recruit. Then the check can match the job.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Which job needs the MOST thorough screening?
options: A receptionist who welcomes visitors and answers the phone
A database administrator for all customer records
A driver who takes the post to each office every morning
An intern who sorts the office supplies on Fridays
options_why: The receptionist has little access to sensitive data.
This job has little access to sensitive data.
The intern has no access to sensitive data.
cards.answer: A database administrator for all customer records
cards.explanation: The more power a job gives over data, the more harm a mistake or a lie can do.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: A company wants to look at the social media of candidates. What does the manual ask for?
options: No rules, because the profiles are public
A ban on all online research about candidates in any country
Clear rules, and telling the candidates about it
A look at the photos only
options_why: Public profiles can still be misused. Rules keep the process fair.
The manual does not ban it. It asks for clear rules.
The rules should decide which information to take, not only photos.
cards.answer: Clear rules, and telling the candidates about it
cards.explanation: Rules prevent abuse and make the method fair for every candidate.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on online background screening.

cards.question: A candidate lies about a degree in the application. Which step can find this?
options: A job description that lists the tasks
A longer interview about the hobbies of the person
A background check that confirms the education
A sign-in code on the first day
options_why: The description lists tasks. It does not check facts.
An interview cannot confirm a degree.
A sign-in code controls access. It does not check the past.
cards.answer: A background check that confirms the education
cards.explanation: A background check confirms the facts in the application, such as education.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: A hiring manager says that there is no time for screening. What is the BEST answer from a CISSP?
options: Agree, because speed matters most for the business
The check must match the risk of the job
Give full access now and check the person later
Refuse to hire anyone without a government clearance
options_why: Speed helps, but a rushed check can bring a risky person inside.
Access before the check is risky. Checking comes first.
This is extreme. Most jobs need a check that fits, not the highest one.
cards.answer: The check must match the risk of the job
cards.explanation: A CISSP thinks about risk. The depth of the check should match the sensitivity of the role.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: As a CISSP, what should you make sure the company has for hiring?
options: One global check that ignores local laws
A fast check that skips the criminal record
A rule to hire only people that the manager knows
Policies to screen and hire under local rules
options_why: Laws about checks differ from place to place. One check for all can break the law.
Skipping a check leaves the company at risk, and local law may ask for it.
Knowing someone is not a check. It can also be unfair.
cards.answer: Policies to screen and hire under local rules
cards.explanation: The manual asks for policies and procedures that follow the rules of your jurisdiction (the area where your laws apply).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: What is the sensitivity level of a job based on? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: The harm that a person in that job could cause, on purpose or by mistake.
cards.explanation: More possible harm means a higher level and a deeper check.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”.

cards.question: Which part of a background check looks at the money of a person?
cards.answer: Credit and financial history.
cards.explanation: It is one of the six points in the list of the manual.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Candidate Screening and Hiring”. The six points: education, work history, citizenship, criminal record, credit and financial history, references.

cards.question: What must a company plan before it looks at the social media of candidates?
cards.answer: Clear rules. They say what to use, which information to keep, how to check that it is true, and how to tell the candidates.
cards.explanation: Fair rules protect both the company and the candidates.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on online background screening.

cards.question: Why must the check go deeper for a sensitive job? Use your own words.
cards.answer: A job with more power can do more harm, by mistake or on purpose. The check must match that risk.
cards.explanation: You check more carefully the person who gets the key to the safe.

concepts.name: Agreements signed by the employee (NDA, noncompete)

decouverte.titre: The secret tactics of the team
paragraphes: You join an online game team. The captain shares the secret tactics of the team. First, he asks for a promise: never tell anyone.
He asks for a second promise: if you leave, do not join the rival team for a while.
In a company, these two promises are written down and signed. They are called the nondisclosure agreement (NDA) and the noncompete agreement.

decouverte.comme: The first promise says: do not repeat our secrets. The second says: do not play for our rivals for a while.
decouverte.enVrai: The NDA protects sensitive information, like trade secrets (secret ways to make a product) and customer files. It often lasts for life. The noncompete protects the company from unfair competition by a former employee, for a fixed time. The image stops here: these are signed contracts, not simple promises.

decouverte.question: An engineer leaves a phone company and shares the secret plans of a future phone. Which agreement was broken?
options: The noncompete
The NDA
Neither of them
decouverte.explanation: Sharing secret information is what the NDA forbids. The noncompete forbids working for a rival.

decouverte.texte: A phone maker hires a hardware engineer. The engineer signs an NDA: no talking about the secret plans. The engineer also signs a noncompete: no work for a rival for eighteen months after leaving.

Employees often sign other rules too. The acceptable use policy says what you may do with company equipment. The code of conduct says how to behave well. The conflict of interest policy says how to keep your own interest apart from the interest of the company.

cards.question: Official definition: “nondisclosure agreement (NDA)”
cards.answer: A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee or contractor (or anyone else with access to sensitive information) from disclosing sensitive information they obtain through the course of their employment or relationship with an organization.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a signed promise not to share the secret information of the company.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “nondisclosure agreement (NDA)”?
options: A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee or contractor (or anyone else with access to sensitive information) from disclosing sensitive information they obtain through the course of their employment or relationship with an organization.
A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee from working for competitors of the organization during and after their employment.

A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that allows an employee or contractor (or anyone else with access to sensitive information) to share sensitive information they obtain with other organizations.

A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee (but not a contractor) from disclosing sensitive information they obtain through the course of their employment with an organization.
options_why: This is the noncompete. The NDA is about sharing information, not about the next employer.
It says the opposite. An NDA restricts sharing, it does not allow it.
It looks close, but the real sentence also covers contractors and anyone else with access.
cards.answer: A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee or contractor (or anyone else with access to sensitive information) from disclosing sensitive information they obtain through the course of their employment or relationship with an organization.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: restricts, disclosing sensitive information, employee or contractor, anyone else with access.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “nondisclosure agreement (NDA)” from memory.
cards.answer: A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is an agreement that restricts an employee or contractor (or anyone else with access to sensitive information) from disclosing sensitive information they obtain through the course of their employment or relationship with an organization.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: who is limited, what they must not reveal, and where the information comes from.

cards.question: Official definition: “noncompete agreement”
cards.answer: A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for a fixed time after employment.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a signed promise not to work against the company, during the job and for a fixed time after.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”. The manual gives an example. A hardware engineer for a phone designer may not work for other phone designers for at least 18 months.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “noncompete agreement”?
options: A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for a fixed time after employment.

A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from disclosing sensitive information of the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for a fixed time after employment.
A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for life after employment.
A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization only after their employment ends.
options_why: This is the NDA. The noncompete is about competing, not about sharing information.
A fixed time is not the same as for life. A lifetime promise fits the NDA better.
The real sentence covers the time during the job too, not only the time after.
cards.answer: A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for a fixed time after employment.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: directly competing, during their employment, a fixed time after employment.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “noncompete agreement” from memory.
cards.answer: A noncompete agreement is an agreement that restricts an employee from directly competing with the organization during their employment and, in most cases, for a fixed time after employment.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: competing directly, during the job, and for a fixed time after it.

cards.question: Official definition: “NDA: purpose and length”
cards.answer: An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).
cards.explanation: In simple words: the NDA keeps company secrets safe, and it often lasts for life, even after the person leaves.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “NDA: purpose and length”?
options: An NDA is designed to protect the availability of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).

An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).

An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a one-year agreement (it ends when the employee leaves the company).

An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the personal data of the employee (such as health records or home address) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).
options_why: Availability is another security goal. The NDA protects confidentiality.
The real sentence says it often lasts for life, even after the employee leaves.
The NDA protects the data of the organization, not the personal data of the employee.
cards.answer: An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: confidentiality, the organization's data, often a lifetime agreement.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “NDA: purpose and length” from memory.
cards.answer: An NDA is designed to protect the confidentiality of the organization's data (such as trade secrets or customer information) and is often a lifetime agreement (even after the employee leaves the company).
cards.explanation: Three blocks: protect confidentiality, a lifetime agreement, even after leaving.

cards.question: Official definition: “purpose of the noncompete”
cards.answer: Noncompetes are one-way agreements that are designed to protect organizations from unfair competition by former employees or contractors.
cards.explanation: In simple words: only the company is protected. The promise goes one way.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “purpose of the noncompete” from memory.
cards.answer: Noncompetes are one-way agreements that are designed to protect organizations from unfair competition by former employees or contractors.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: one-way, protect organizations, against unfair competition.

cards.question: A former employee tells a newspaper the secret recipe of the company. Which agreement was broken?
options: The noncompete
The acceptable use policy
The NDA
The conflict of interest policy
options_why: The noncompete is about working for a rival. Nobody worked for a rival here.
This policy is about how to use company equipment, not about sharing secrets.
This policy is about mixing personal and company interests, not about sharing secrets.
cards.answer: The NDA
cards.explanation: Sharing secret information is exactly what the NDA forbids.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: A former employee joins a rival company one month after leaving. Which agreement is involved?
options: The NDA
The acceptable use policy
The code of conduct
The noncompete
options_why: The NDA is about sharing secrets. Nothing says that a secret was shared.
This policy is about company equipment, not about the next employer.
It is about good behavior at work, not about the next employer.
cards.answer: The noncompete
cards.explanation: The person now works for a competitor. The noncompete is the agreement that forbids this.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: How long does an NDA often last?
options: Often for life, even after the person leaves
Only for the time that the person works there
For one year after the person leaves
Until the end of the current year
options_why: The person still knows the secrets after leaving, so the promise goes on.
A fixed time after leaving fits the noncompete better.
An NDA does not stop on a calendar date.
cards.answer: Often for life, even after the person leaves
cards.explanation: Secrets stay secret, even when the person has left the company.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”. The manual says the NDA is often a lifetime agreement.

cards.question: Who does a noncompete protect?
options: The employee, who gets paid extra for the promise
Both sides in the same way
The company, because it is a one-way agreement
The customers of the company
options_why: The manual says the noncompete protects organizations, not employees.
It is one-way: only the organization is protected.
Customers are not the target. The company is protected from unfair competition.
cards.answer: The company, because it is a one-way agreement
cards.explanation: The employee makes a promise, and the company is the one that is protected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: Which sentence about an NDA is NOT true?
options: It can protect trade secrets
It stops the employee from working for a rival
It can protect customer information held by the company
It can last after the employee leaves
options_why: This is true. Trade secrets are a main example.
This is true. The manual gives it as an example.
This is true. Many NDAs last for life.
cards.answer: It stops the employee from working for a rival
cards.explanation: Working for a rival is the job of the noncompete. The NDA is about sharing information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: A company will hire an engineer who will see secret plans. Which agreement is the BEST way to protect the confidentiality of the plans?
options: A noncompete signed after the engineer leaves
A code of conduct without any other paper
A conflict of interest policy signed next year
An NDA signed before the engineer starts
options_why: A noncompete limits who the person works for. It does not keep the plans secret.
A code of conduct sets behavior. It does not keep secrets by itself.
This policy is late and is about interests, not about secrets.
cards.answer: An NDA signed before the engineer starts
cards.explanation: The NDA is the tool that protects the confidentiality of company data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: A phone maker asks an engineer not to work for other phone makers for 18 months after leaving. What is the MOST likely goal?
options: To protect the company from unfair competition
To keep customer data secret
To teach the engineer the rules of the company
To stop the engineer from using company computers
options_why: That is the goal of an NDA, not of a noncompete.
Teaching rules is the job of training, not of this agreement.
This is the job of the acceptable use policy.
cards.answer: To protect the company from unfair competition
cards.explanation: After 18 months, the inside knowledge of the engineer is less of an edge for a rival.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: A new contractor will see trade secrets. What should the company ask the contractor to do FIRST?
options: Start work now and sign the papers later
Read the secrets and then decide on an NDA
Promise not to join a rival after the job
Sign an NDA before the work starts
options_why: Secrets could be shared before the promise exists.
By then, the secrets are already known.
A noncompete helps later, but the secrets need protection first.
cards.answer: Sign an NDA before the work starts
cards.explanation: An NDA also covers contractors. It sets the expectations before they see anything.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: An employee uses a company laptop to download games. Which signed rule is involved?
options: The NDA
The acceptable use policy
The noncompete
The conflict of interest policy
options_why: No secret was shared, so the NDA is not involved.
The employee does not work for a rival.
Personal interest is not set against the company here.
cards.answer: The acceptable use policy
cards.explanation: This policy says what you may do with company equipment.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”. Outside the manual: the simple explanations of each policy are ours.

cards.question: A manager picks a supplier owned by her brother and tells nobody. Which policy covers this?
options: The acceptable use policy for company equipment
The noncompete
The conflict of interest policy
The NDA
options_why: It is about company equipment, not about choosing a supplier.
No rival is involved here.
No secret was shared here.
cards.answer: The conflict of interest policy
cards.explanation: Her own interest (her brother) is mixed with the interest of the company.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”. Outside the manual: the simple explanations of each policy are ours.

cards.question: What does an NDA protect? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: The confidentiality of company data, like trade secrets and customer information.
cards.explanation: Think of the promise not to tell the secret tactics of the team.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: Who is helped by a noncompete: the company or the employee?
cards.answer: The company. It is a one-way agreement.
cards.explanation: The employee makes a promise to the company, and the company makes no promise back.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Employment Agreements and Policies”.

cards.question: What is an acceptable use policy for?
cards.answer: It says what you may do with company equipment.
cards.explanation: Think of the rules for using the school computers.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: the manual only names this policy. The simple explanation is ours.

cards.question: What is a conflict of interest policy for?
cards.answer: It says how to keep your own interest apart from the interest of the company.
cards.explanation: Think of a judge who must not judge a case about a close friend.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: the manual only names this policy. The simple explanation is ours.

cards.question: What does a code of conduct say?
cards.answer: It says how to behave well at work.
cards.explanation: It is the list of good habits of the company.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: the manual only names this policy. The simple explanation is ours.

paragraphes: At the start of the year, you get a timetable, a locker and the rules. Someone tells you who to ask if there is a problem.
A few months later, you change class. Your old key to the science room should not open that door any more.
In a company, these two moments are called onboarding (joining) and transfer (changing role). Each one has its own security rules.

decouverte.titre: The rules at the start of the year
decouverte.comme: On day one, the rules are explained. You know what to do. You also know that cameras watch the playground.
decouverte.enVrai: Onboarding teaches a new employee to protect information. It shows how to report an incident. It shows how to see the sensitivity level (the classification) of information. The employee also learns that the company may watch how its assets are used. The image stops here: you do not give the technical details of this watching.

decouverte.question: An employee changes department. What should happen to the old access?
options: Keep it, just in case
Remove what is no longer needed
Double it
decouverte.answer: Remove what is no longer needed
decouverte.explanation: Extra access is an open door for no reason. This is least privilege: each person gets only the access that the job needs.

decouverte.texte: Karim worked in accounting and could see salaries. Now he moves to sales. He does not need the salary files any more, so his access is removed. Before the move, he takes training for the sales software and for customer data. This is role-based training: lessons for the new role.

cards.question: Official definition: “the three stages of employment”
cards.answer: Onboarding, transfers, and termination are three stages of employment that each comes with its own security considerations.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a person joins, changes role, and leaves. Each moment has its own security rules.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding, Transfers, and Termination Processes”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “the three stages of employment”?

cards.question: Say the official definition of “transfers” from memory.
cards.answer: Organizations should have well-defined policies and procedures for handling an employee transferring from one role to another.

cards.question: On day one, a new employee learns how to report a security incident. Which stage is this?

Screening
Onboarding

cards.answer: Onboarding

cards.question: An employee moves from support to sales. Which stage is this?
options: Transfer
Onboarding
Termination
Screening

cards.answer: Transfer

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: What should a new employee learn about monitoring?
options: The technical details, so they understand the controls
Nothing, because secret monitoring works better
That controls exist which watch how assets are used
Only that cameras exist in the halls
options_why: The goal is not to give enough detail to get around the controls.
Knowing about it is reassuring and can stop bad behavior.
The controls cover all company assets, not only cameras.
cards.answer: That controls exist which watch how assets are used
cards.explanation: The employee must know that actions may be reviewed, without knowing how to beat the controls.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”.

cards.question: What should happen to old access when an employee gets a new role?
options: All old access stays, in case it is needed
Old access stays until the employee asks to remove it
Access that is no longer needed is removed
Old access is doubled to help with the move
options_why: Old access that is not needed is an open door. It breaks least privilege.
Nobody should wait to be asked. The company must review the access.
More access means more risk, not less.
cards.answer: Access that is no longer needed is removed
cards.explanation: This is least privilege: each person keeps only the access that the new job needs.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: An employee will move from support to database administrator, with more sensitive data. What should the company do FIRST?
options: Let the employee learn on the job
Give the employee all the access of the new team
Wait one year before any training
Find the role-based training the employee needs

Giving all access breaks least privilege.
Waiting leaves the employee unprepared with sensitive data.
cards.answer: Find the role-based training the employee needs
cards.explanation: The manual wants role-based training before the transfer, most of all for more sensitive data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: Karim moves from accounting to sales. What is the BEST action for his access to the salary files?
options: Keep it for a few months, just in case
Remove it, because the new role does not need it
Keep it, because he is a trusted and loyal employee
Keep it, but ask him not to use it

A promise is weaker than removing the access.
cards.answer: Remove it, because the new role does not need it
cards.explanation: Least privilege: remove the access that the new role will not need.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: Which topic is NOT a good part of security onboarding?
options: Details that would help to beat the monitoring
How to report a security incident that you see at work

The role of the employee in keeping the work area safe

This is good. The manual asks for it.
This is good. The manual asks for it.

cards.explanation: The aim is to show that actions may be reviewed, not to give enough detail to beat the controls.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”.

cards.question: Which reason is the MOST useful for telling new employees that they may be watched?
options: It lets employees test the controls by themselves
It may stop bad behavior and gives assurance
It removes the need for access controls
It replaces the need to report incidents

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”.

cards.question: Which step does the LEAST to keep least privilege during a transfer?
options: Reviewing the access the employee has now
Asking if the old access is still needed
Adding the new access on top of all the old access
Removing the access that the new role does not need at all

This is exactly what least privilege asks for.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: When does the manual say that good work behavior should start to be set?
options: On the first day at work
After the first month of work
After the first security incident of the year
Before the employee walks in the door
options_why: The manual says even earlier.
This is too late to set expectations.
Waiting for an incident means acting too late.
cards.answer: Before the employee walks in the door
cards.explanation: Good expectations start before the first day.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”.

cards.question: Why must a new employee learn how to see the sensitivity level of information?

To decide on their own who may see the information
To know which files can be deleted
To know how long the files must be kept

Keeping time is a different topic.
cards.answer: To know how much control the information needs
cards.explanation: The level tells the employee how strongly the information must be protected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”. The manual calls this the classification and categorization process.

cards.question: What do new employees learn about incidents during onboarding?
cards.answer: How to report a security incident.
cards.explanation: A fast report can stop a small problem from growing.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Onboarding”.

cards.question: What is role-based training?
cards.answer: Lessons for the tasks and the data of a new role.
cards.explanation: Karim learns the sales software before he moves to sales.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”. Outside the manual: the simple explanation is ours.

cards.question: What does a transfer do to the old access of the employee?
cards.answer: It is reviewed. What the new role no longer needs is removed.
cards.explanation: Every extra access is a door left open for nothing.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Transfers”.

cards.question: What is least privilege, in your own words?
cards.answer: Give each person only the access that the job needs.
cards.explanation: Think of the keys of the school: each person has only the keys they need.

paragraphes: You leave a sports club. You give back your badge and the key to your locker. The club also cuts your access to the booking app.

A company follows the same habits each time someone leaves. This is called termination, chosen or not.

decouverte.comme: The club has a list: badge back, key back, access cut, door code changed.
decouverte.enVrai: When someone leaves, the company suspends electronic access, takes back badges and equipment, counts the keys and changes the lock codes. Equipment may be kept as evidence for forensic analysis (a search for traces on devices). A person who has left is a former insider: someone who knew the inside of the company. The image stops here: a forced departure needs more care than a calm one.

Right away, when the news is given
After one week, to hand over the work
decouverte.answer: Right away, when the news is given
decouverte.explanation: The company must assume that a fired person may be a threat. Access that stays on is an open door.

decouverte.texte: A technician is fired. Before leaving, the technician copies customer files. The plan is to sell the files to a rival. Or it may lock the data with ransomware. Ransomware is a program that locks data until you pay. A tool called UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) watches for unusual actions of users. It could have warned the company.

cards.question: Official definition: “voluntary and involuntary termination”
cards.answer: Terminations may be voluntary (i.e., an employee retires or finds a new job) or involuntary (i.e., an employee is fired, furloughed, or otherwise "let go").
cards.explanation: In simple words: voluntary means the person chooses to leave. Involuntary means the company decides.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”. Furloughed means sent home on forced leave.

cards.question: Official definition: “involuntary termination”
cards.answer: In virtually all cases, an involuntary termination forces the employer to assume the terminated individual is a threat to the organization, and appropriate action should be taken to protect organizational assets.
cards.explanation: In simple words: when a person is sent away, the company assumes that person may be a threat. It must protect what has value for the company (its assets).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

options: In virtually all cases, a voluntary termination forces the employer to assume the terminated individual is a threat to the organization, and appropriate action should be taken to protect organizational assets.

In virtually all cases, an involuntary termination forces the employer to assume the terminated individual is a threat to the organization, and appropriate action should be taken to protect organizational assets.

cards.question: Official definition: “former insiders”
cards.answer: These former insiders represent a risk to the organization, and appropriate actions must be taken to ensure they do not compromise the operations, intellectual property, or sensitive information with which they have been entrusted.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “former insiders” from memory.
cards.answer: These former insiders represent a risk to the organization, and appropriate actions must be taken to ensure they do not compromise the operations, intellectual property, or sensitive information with which they have been entrusted.

cards.question: Official definition: “termination procedures”

cards.question: Say the official definition of “termination procedures” from memory.
cards.answer: Termination procedures at most organizations include specific processes to notify the information security organization to disable access to electronic and physical systems.

cards.question: Which of these is a voluntary termination?
options: An employee retires
An employee is fired
An employee is furloughed (sent home on forced leave)
A company lets an employee go
options_why: Being fired is the choice of the company, so it is involuntary.

cards.question: Why can a former employee be a risk?
options: The person gets more access after leaving the company
The person now owns the company data
The person knows the inside of the company
The person will always want revenge

The data belongs to the company, not to the person.
Not everyone is angry. But the company must still be careful.
cards.answer: The person knows the inside of the company

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: Which action is on the standard checklist when an employee leaves on good terms?
options: Suspend electronic access and collect badges and equipment
Leave the access on for a full week as a courtesy to the person
Keep the lock codes unchanged
Let the person keep the company laptop

The lock codes the person used must be changed.
Company equipment must be taken back.
cards.answer: Suspend electronic access and collect badges and equipment

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: A manager fires an employee who still has access to the customer database. What should happen FIRST?

Disable the access when the news is given
Ask the employee to bring back the badge next week
Tell the customers about the firing
options_why: Every hour with access is a risk. Waiting means acting too late.
The badge matters, but the electronic access is the faster danger.
Customers do not need to know. The access must be cut first.
cards.answer: Disable the access when the news is given
cards.explanation: The company must assume that a fired person may be a threat, so access is cut right away.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: What is the BEST way to treat an employee who is fired after an argument?
options: Trust the person, because they worked there for years
Let the person keep access to finish the work
Tell the team that the person is a thief
Assume the person may be a threat and protect the assets
options_why: Years of work do not remove the risk of an angry former insider.
Access that stays on is an open door.
Protect the assets without accusing. A guess is not a proof.
cards.answer: Assume the person may be a threat and protect the assets
cards.explanation: Caution protects the company without judging the person.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: Which action is NOT part of the advice of the manual for an involuntary termination?
options: Telling the security team to disable access
Recovering the property the person used
Telling the staff that the person has no more access
Keeping access on so the work can be handed over

This is advised, where possible.
This is advised, with a request to report any attempt to get in.
cards.answer: Keeping access on so the work can be handed over

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: Which sign should worry a security team MOST when an angry employee is about to leave?

The employee takes a long lunch

The employee joins a team meeting

This is a normal question.
This is normal work.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: After someone is fired, what should the rest of the staff be told?
options: Nothing, to avoid a fuss
The person has lost access, so report any attempt
The detailed reasons for the firing
The person may come back for their things at any time
options_why: Without this information, nobody notices an attempt to get in.

Free entry goes against protecting the assets.
cards.answer: The person has lost access, so report any attempt
cards.explanation: The staff become a security relay: they report any unusual attempt.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: What is the BEST reason to track the property of a fired employee as evidence?

It teaches the person a lesson
It may help a later forensic analysis
It lets the company reuse the old passwords

cards.question: What does a UEBA tool do?

It stores the backups of the company in a safe place
It checks the degrees of new hires
It studies user behavior to spot unusual actions

cards.question: A company fires a technician but forgets to tell the security team. What is the main danger?

The other staff will not be told about the departure of the person
The access may stay on and be used to cause harm

cards.question: Why is a fired employee treated as a possible threat?

cards.explanation: Caution protects the company without accusing the person.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: What does UEBA stand for?
cards.answer: User and Entity Behavior Analytics. It helps to spot unusual behavior.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”. See the Tip box.

cards.question: What should be done with property taken back from a fired employee, when it is right to do so?
cards.answer: Track it as evidence and keep it for forensic analysis (a search for traces on devices).
cards.explanation: The equipment may hold useful traces if something went wrong.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: Who must be told when someone is fired, so that access is cut?

cards.explanation: It can then disable electronic and physical access.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”.

cards.question: What does “furloughed” mean?
cards.answer: Sent home on forced leave.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Termination”. Outside the manual: the manual uses the word without explaining it.

cards.question: A company keeps its privacy policy in a locked drawer in the management office. What is the BEST fix?
options: Make the policy available to all personnel
Encrypt the policy
Keep it secret, like a trade secret
Send it to the customers every month
options_why: Encryption is not the issue. The problem is that staff cannot read it.
The policy explains practices. It does not have to stay secret.
The manual does not ask for a monthly mailing.
cards.answer: Make the policy available to all personnel
cards.explanation: The manual asks that all personnel can read it, and often that each person signs an acknowledgment.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: A company starts to collect personal data from people in the EU. What should it do FIRST for its privacy policy?
options: Collect the data and write the policy next year
Copy the privacy policy of another company
Link it to the laws that apply, such as GDPR
Ask each customer to write the policy
options_why: Writing the policy late is reactive. Prevent problems first.
Another company has other data and other practices.
The company writes its own policy.
cards.answer: Link it to the laws that apply, such as GDPR
cards.explanation: A policy that links to the right laws shows which rules the company follows.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: Which policy MOST helps people to know how their personal data is used?
options: The acceptable use policy
The privacy policy
The conflict of interest policy
The code of conduct
options_why: This policy is about how staff use company equipment.
This policy is about personal interest against company interest.
This policy is about good behavior at work.
cards.answer: The privacy policy
cards.explanation: The privacy policy explains the collection and use practices for personal data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: Which topic is NOT part of what a privacy policy should explain?
options: What kind of personal data is collected
How the company will or will not use the data
The salaries of the managers
How the data will be stored and secured
options_why: This is part of it. The manual names it first.
This is part of it. The manual names it second.
This is part of it. The manual names it third.
cards.answer: The salaries of the managers
cards.explanation: The policy is about personal data practices: collection, use, storage and security.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: A sports app writes: “We take your name and heart rate. We use them for your statistics. We do not sell them. They are encrypted on our servers.” Which sentence tells how the data is protected?
options: They are encrypted on our servers
We take your name and heart rate
We use them for your statistics
We do not sell them
options_why: This sentence says what is collected.
This sentence says how the data is used.
This sentence also says how the data is used.
cards.answer: They are encrypted on our servers
cards.explanation: Encrypted means locked with a secret key. This is how the app keeps the data safe.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”. Outside the manual: the sports app is our example.

cards.question: Many organizations ask each employee to sign something about the privacy policy. What is it?
options: A new noncompete agreement
A signed acknowledgment
A copy of their personal data
An NDA for each customer
options_why: A noncompete is about competition, not about the privacy policy.
The employee does not sign a copy of data.
The acknowledgment is about the employee, not about each customer.
cards.answer: A signed acknowledgment
cards.explanation: The acknowledgment shows that the employee has the policy.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: What does a privacy policy say about collection?
cards.answer: What kind of personal data is collected.
cards.explanation: This is the first of three parts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: What does a privacy policy say about use?
cards.answer: How the organization will or will not use the personal data.
cards.explanation: This is the second of three parts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: What does a privacy policy say about protection?
cards.answer: How the personal data will be stored, kept and secured.
cards.explanation: This is the third of three parts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.

cards.question: Which laws should a privacy policy point to?
cards.answer: The privacy laws that apply. For example HIPAA in the United States, or GDPR for EU residents.
cards.explanation: The policy shows which laws it relies on.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Privacy Policy Requirements”.
